tagline: Steep grades cross high mountain country beside a sacred stone wheel.
intro: Medicine Wheel Passage follows 27 miles of two-lane paved highway across the northern Bighorn National Forest. The road winds steeply, with truck turnoffs and grades reaching 10 percent. The Forest Service describes the scenic byway as a journey through high-elevation plains and deep canyons, with fishing, waterfalls and cultural sites. A viewpoint at 9,430 feet looks southwest into the Big Horn Basin. Heavy snow closes this crossing in winter and early spring, leaving summer and fall as its driving seasons. Elevation changes along the way bring a variety of habitats, from timber stands to springs in the forest.

The road’s number changed as the main highway shifted. In 1940, US 14 moved south to its present alignment; the old alignment became Wyoming 14 before being recommissioned as US 14A around 1965. That numbered route extends from Cody to Burgess Junction, while the 27-mile scenic byway runs between the western forest boundary and Burgess Junction.

From the western forest boundary, travel east toward the Medicine Wheel turnoff, then the Bald Mountain City pullout and the North Tongue River. The river forms grassy meadows and cuts through granite canyons on the eastern stretch. At Burgess Junction, US 14A meets US 14 and the Big Horn Scenic Byway.

moments.title: Medicine Wheel
moments.text: Local white limestone forms the Medicine Wheel on Medicine Mountain, a place of sacred ceremony as well as scientific inquiry. Twenty-eight stone spokes connect its outer ring with a central cairn. The site is sacred to people of many nations. The Arapaho call it Hiieeinoonotii; during landmark-status negotiations, the Crow stated that the wheel was already present when they arrived in the area. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1970, and its name expanded to Medicine Wheel/Medicine Mountain in 2011. The approach leaves the highway on a short gravel road to a parking area, followed by a three-mile round-trip walk.
moments.notice: A ring of limestone boulders surrounds 28 spokes and a central cairn.

moments.title: Bald Mountain City
moments.text: Gold-bearing quartz in the local granite drew prospectors to Bald Mountain City. In the 1890s they staked claims, built mines and founded towns. The harsh climate and low gold yield ended the operation after a few years, leaving place names behind. A highway pullout at the ghost-town site has interpretive signs explaining the mining history.

moments.title: North Tongue River
moments.text: On the eastern stretch of Medicine Wheel Passage, the North Tongue River forms grassy meadows and carves canyons through granite beside the highway. The meadows offer opportunities for trout fishing and moose viewing. Farther east, Burgess Junction marks the meeting with the Bighorn Scenic Byway, with high meadows and conifers near its visitor center.
